title: Strain-Induced Helical Superconductivity and the Zero-Field Diode Effect
abstract: Motivated by the strain-induced zero-field superconducting diode effect observed in PbTaSe$_2$, we identify a mechanism by which strain generates nonreciprocal superconducting transport without magnetism or an external magnetic field. Uniaxial strain mixes a dominant $s$-wave order parameter with a subdominant two-component pairing channel and enhances their symmetry-allowed Lifshitz coupling. Beyond a critical strain, this coupling drives a transition into a helical state with spontaneously selected finite Cooper-pair momentum and broken time-reversal symmetry. The resulting diode effect is generically non-monotonic in strain and exhibits distinct responses for currents parallel and perpendicular to the residual mirror plane, consistent with experiment. Our theory predicts that reversing the principal strain switches the diode direction by $90^\circ$, while shear strain rotates it continuously. These results establish strain as a symmetry-selective means of creating, controlling, and diagnosing spontaneous helical superconductivity.
summary: This theoretical work establishes that mechanical strain can induce a zero-field superconducting diode effect by driving the system into a helical superconducting state. Using a Ginzburg-Landau approach, the authors show that strain mixes s-wave pairing with higher-order channels, leading to spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking and a measurable diode response. This provides a strain-tunable method for controlling superconducting transport properties.
main_problem: The paper addresses the mechanism behind the zero-field superconducting diode effect (SDE) induced purely by mechanical strain, without requiring external magnetic fields or magnetism.
main_result: Uniaxial strain drives a superconducting transition into a helical state characterized by spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking and a finite Cooper-pair momentum, which generates the measurable diode effect.
method: The analysis employs a symmetry-based Ginzburg-Landau free energy expansion, modeling the superconducting order parameter using multiple components.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using a Ginzburg-Landau theory for superconductors, specifically investigating materials like PbTaSe2. The theory incorporates strain ($\epsilon$) effects and symmetry-allowed Lifshitz coupling terms acting on two superconducting order parameters.
key_observables: Non-reciprocal critical current (SDE), spontaneous Cooper-pair momentum ($q^*$), and the strain dependence of the critical temperature ($T_c(\epsilon)$).
important_parameters: Uniaxial strain ($\epsilon$), the ratio $\gamma(\ell^2 - \xi_2^2)/\xi_2^1$, and the field-free SDE efficiency ($\Delta J_c/J_c$).
main_assumptions: The calculated critical currents are treated as intrinsic depairing currents, ignoring dissipation from vortex motion, and assuming the current does not alter the spontaneous symmetry breaking.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the helical state, the free energy dependence on momentum ($f(q)$), and the strain dependence of the normalized critical currents and the SDE.
paper_structure: The paper builds the theory by first establishing the Ginzburg-Landau framework incorporating strain and Lifshitz coupling. It then analyzes the transition to the helical state, derives the momentum $q^*$, and finally predicts the strain-dependent, non-monotonic behavior of the zero-field SDE.
why_interesting: The mechanism relies on symmetry breaking induced by strain to generate non-reciprocal transport, which is a key concept in topological superconductivity and superconducting electronics, linking structural mechanics to quantum transport.
